sentences.sentence: With no taxation and the ability to own unlimited amounts of firepower, Idaho was a no-brainer.
I was getting ready to fight, not sit on my ass in a safe house in the middle of Idaho.
I threw my rifle over my shoulder and headed out.
The entire city had gone dark, lights blown out, the city grid cut off.
The buildings were eerie in their silence, no one was on the streets, no one was coming out to fight.
Maybe they knew they’d lose.
Maybe they wanted to save themselves and their families and let the big guys fight it out.
I ran through the city, dodging from cover to cover, and jumped behind an old car in front of an abandoned convenience store.
I put my rifle to my shoulder and scanned the street, looking for Ssum units, and saw them coming up the block.
I watched as a half-dozen Ssum dropped from their landing craft and sprinted to cover.
They wore full armor like I did, and were armed like me, with an assault rifle and a pistol.
They were probably part of the Ssum's Special Forces, the best the Ssum had.
I watched them spread out and fan out into the buildings, covering each other and the rest of their unit.
I had been taught as a kid that I should be able to tell what my enemy was thinking just by looking at him.
I had also been taught that sometimes just knowing what your enemy is thinking isn’t enough, that sometimes you have to do something about it.
I leaned out from behind the car and took a quick shot, it was a head shot and I watched the Ssum drop.
The rest of his unit returned fire, and I rolled away from the car and behind the building.

sentences.sentence: was in the thick of it all.
She wasn't a particularly good leader though, and was losing it.
`` We tried to be nice about this, but there's no room left for mercy.
If you don't-'' she paused, scrunched her brow in contemplation, and raised a finger.
`` Actually, we will not compromise.
We will kill you!''
All the gods cheered.
All but one, that is.
It wouldn't have even been as noticeable as that, if she hadn't been right on top of him.
Odin took it as an opportunity, though, and tried to make the best of it.
He looked up at her and cleared his throat.
`` Why would you do that?''
Everyone looked up at him.
Even God.
He'd noticed something about this one.
He wasn't your typical, one-god.
He had that look in his eye.
The look that said he wasn't just there to get his rocks off at someone else's expense.
This was some sort of sick, twisted game going on.
Like a twisted game of cat and mouse, where the cats were people and God was the mouse.
He wasn't sure if he was rooting for the guy, or not, though.
The cats were much more entertaining, anyways.
`` Why would you do that?
You know we don't have anything else to do.''
Odin raised an eyebrow, as his eye had already done.
`` Actually, I thought that was the whole point.
You don't work, you know.
You can't die.
You just have all this time you could fill up with something.
How about you try making a game out of your eternity?''
God just stared blankly.

sentences.sentence: magazines and coffee table book (my dentist is a baseball fan).
And, if I looked closely enough, I could make out a faint odor of Listerine.
The only difference is that I was in a black, seemingly endless, room with no windows.
No clues.
Just a TV, a vending machine, and a couple of the aforementioned chairs.
In fact, the only clue that anyone was anywhere else was a faint noise coming from a door on the opposite wall.
I knew I hadn't heard a door in the regular dentist's waiting room, so I got up to investigate.
As I got close, I realized that the sound I'd heard was something like the sound of a child's crying, or a woman screaming.
I reached the door just as a couple of orderlies were entering with a gurney containing a man.
"Welcome, sir," said one of them as they stopped at the door.
He looked at me.
"You've arrived at the right time.
He'll be awake in a minute."
I backed away nervously.
"I didn't sign up for this.
Sorry guys.
I don't want to participate.
Can I go home?"
"I'm afraid that's not possible.
You're here until we need you.
Now, don't be scared.
He just had a little setback.
It'll be over soon."
Then, the door opened slightly and the two men began dragging the gurney down the hall.
I followed cautiously behind, and when I reached the other side, I looked into the next room.
On the bed was a man, with two IV's sticking out of his arm.
The thing that scared me the most, however, was his head.

sentences.sentence: Dove, better than the Man-O-War, better than the Bubble Man and the Tail Woman; Tony was the best.
He was my cousin.
When Tony died, he left me a letter.
My mom opened it in the kitchen and then went to sit by herself.
I thought that was weird.
"Come on Mom, let's read the letter" I remember saying.
I wanted to know about Tony's life.
When my mom finally opened the letter, she started crying.
That was really weird, but I thought she was upset that Tony had died.
Then, my mom handed me the letter.
It was a big folded page, all typed on a type writer, and it went on for pages.
And then, it stopped.
There was an empty space, with a hand written note at the end.
The note said `` Sorry, your parents wouldn't have wanted you to read this part'' and the letter had been carefully cut to remove the last few pages.
My mom wouldn't tell me anything about it, and she didn't want me to open it.
I did, anyway, because Tony was my cousin and that meant he was in my family.
I opened the letter and read.
I can't remember what happened after that, except that when I went home and tried to tell my parents what I read, my dad broke my head.
My mom didn't even listen to me.

I asked.

I ll get him'

I mumbled.

sentences.sentence: day I was in a lab with other med students to get some of our equipment checked.
A doctor walked in, 6'4", with a beard that wasn't full but looked like he had to shave once a week, hair cut, and glasses.
He walked up and put his hand out to shake mine, I introduced myself, he asked if I had any experience with blood, I replied no.
He said he was the head doctor here, and showed me to the machine and explained what to do.
I didn't listen to his directions and watched him work instead.
After he left I gave the machine a go on myself and proceeded to pass out, I hit my head, then felt it.
The feeling of something sticking in my skull.
The machine didn't work properly apparently, it was supposed to inject me with blood but instead stuck the needle to my brain.
This was the start of me being a doctor.

I spent 15 years doing surgery after surgery, learning to see things other doctors couldn't see, I could look at a picture of someone and instantly diagnose them without talking to them, seeing all the diseases in someone's body, and it took it's toll.
I became one of the most gifted doctors in the world, able to take on any surgery and get them out in under a month.
People from all around would call and ask for my assistance.
I'd been called the best there ever was, even the best ever to live, but I knew I was only the best that lived because I was the best one alive.
So I called it.
